title: Palindrome String

concept.title: Two indexes meeting in the middle
body: A word is a palindrome if the first character equals the last, the second equals the one before the last, and so on. You do not need a reversed copy for that: keep **two indexes**, `i` at the start and `j` at the end, compare the two characters, then move both inward.

body.code:
i = 0
j = len(s) - 1
while i < j:
    # compare s[i] and s[j]
    i += 1
    j -= 1

body: The loop stops when the indexes meet or cross: the middle character of an odd-length word needs no partner. If any pair differs, the answer is "no" and you can stop at once.
Using two indexes that walk towards each other is a pattern you will meet again, in problems about sorted arrays and sums of pairs.

statement: You are given a word. Print `yes` if it reads the same forwards and backwards, otherwise print `no`. Upper and lower case letters are different.
inputFormat: A single word `s` of English letters and digits.

examples.note: L and l are different characters: not a palindrome.

hints: Compare the first character with the last one, the second with the second to last, and so on.
Keep two indexes `i` and `j`. Start with `i = 0` and `j = length - 1`, and loop while `i < j`.
When a pair differs, record `no` and leave the loop with `break`. If the loop ends without a difference, the answer is `yes`.

explanation: The two indexes walk towards the middle. The first mismatching pair proves the word is not a palindrome; if all pairs match, it is one. Only half of the characters are visited.

code.python:
s = input().strip()

i = 0
j = len(s) - 1
answer = "yes"
while i < j:
    if s[i] != s[j]:
        answer = "no"
        break
    i += 1
    j -= 1
print(answer)
